_about: The household-work page's figures (feature 231), from the diagram research answer to diagram#21 (questions 0311-0317, verified on diagram main at aa9bbeb). Every figure carries the verdict the research gave it and its question file; l7r/money/household.py checks both. Prose that frames them lives in templates/money_household.html.

year.scope: One holding of 1 cho 2 tan 5 se (about 1.2 hectares), a samurai who farmed his own land, in Iyo between 1629 and 1654, by the Seiryoki; larger than most farms. Night work is not counted, and the women's days are one lump of field labor.

hypothesis.says: No. A household's own cloth took about 51 days a year, against over 200 women's field days for a cho of paddy. Cotton, two historians argue, freed women's time for the fields.

Perhaps. Ramie took nearly ten times the labor of cotton by one historian's estimate; at ten times, the same cloth would take about 512 days, more than one woman's year (the research project's arithmetic).
Only cloth for sale is counted: a woman spinning and weaving about 200 days a year was at the practical maximum, about level with a small farm's field year. A household's own clothes are not timed.
Yes. The holding's 811 counted days and the women's 200-odd far exceed the cloth's 51.
No: wives probably worked almost as many days for income as their husbands.

city.says: Only the rice polishers could sell white rice; about 1,100 polished it in the street in 1727.
Rice 200 mon a day and miso and soy sauce 50, from a vegetable peddler's takings (Bunsei era, 1818-30).
About 128 monme: rent 10, food for a couple and a child about 30, seasonings and firewood together 58, the rest tools, furniture and clothing (Bunsei era).
Sushi 8 mon a piece and egg omelette 16 at street stalls, three or four stalls a block where people were about at night.
8 mon an adult from 1841 (a tenement had no bath); 24 by 1866 as firewood grew dear.
Much of a commoner's clothing was bought secondhand; 220 licensed buyers walked Edo's streets in 1659. No price was found.
Washing shops by about 1688; no price, and no account of whose clothes they washed.
A tenement's water was piped to a shared well; elsewhere people bought river water from sellers. No price was found.
No trade that mended a household's clothes, and no price, was found.

classes.says: One holding's year is counted task by task (above), with night work and the women's household work left out. No source splits a farm household's year among its members.

classes.who: A city laborer, single or with a family
classes.says: No source counts a city household's own work, for a single man in a back tenement or for a family. Both budgets found are family men's. One writer, citing nothing, says married peddlers worked every day while single ones rested when they liked.

classes.who: A live-in servant, apprentice or clerk
classes.says: No household of their own to work for: they lived in the shop until head clerk. Leave home was a few days after New Year and at Bon (yabuiri), sometimes with pocket money and new clothes. Whether they traded on the side is not recorded.

classes.who: A samurai posted alone to a lord's Edo compound
classes.says: Cooked for himself or ate out, and often used the public baths.

classes.who: A porter, a guard or a footman
classes.says: What they did on their days off is not recorded.

woman_day.scope: The Imai, wealthy farmers of Shinano, 1821: a day laborer was paid 50 mon if a man, 16 to 33 mon if a woman.
